images.prompt: Photorealistic macro photograph of a handcrafted miniature tabletop diorama. A small interview table of brushed graphite, about the width of a hardback book, stands at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop. On one side, two empty graphite chairs sit side by side; facing them across the table is a single chair, its ivory seat pad still dented. On the table lies a graphite clipboard holding an ivory audit form of blank tick boxes, a pen resting across it. The one acid-lime element is an unmarked removal tag on a thin thread, lying beside the clipboard, ready to be used. Behind the table, four miniature graphite desks stand in a neat row, each with a cold frosted mug or a folded jacket left on it. Eraser crumbs and pencil dust mark the form. Wide 16:9 landscape frame. The hero object sits slightly left of centre on the lower third, with the related objects extending to the right so the workflow reads left to right. Clean, generous negative space above. Shot as a real physical model, not a 3D render. Materials are limited and tactile: heavyweight ivory cotton paper and card with visible fibres, soft folds and slightly deckled edges; matte, bead-blasted graphite metal with fine machining lines, chamfered edges and tiny hex fasteners; frosted acrylic with milky edges and a soft internal glow; sandblasted frosted glass. Surfaces carry believable imperfections: fine dust, paper grain, hairline creases, light scuffs on metal. Every object has convincing miniature scale and weight and rests firmly on its surface. Colour palette is restrained and nearly monochrome: white #FFFFFF, warm ivory, pale neutral #F3F5F2, soft grey-green #DCE1DA, muted graphite #626A64 and deep graphite #191D1B. Acid lime #D0F344 appears only on the lime element named in the scene, as the single signal colour, with olive #718D0B on its shadowed sides. Nothing else is lime or saturated; no red, orange or blue accents. Lighting: one large soft key light from the upper left at about 45 degrees, like diffused north-window daylight, with a gentle white bounce fill from the right; soft grounded contact shadows fall to the lower right. Camera: 100mm macro lens at f/4, eye level with the tabletop, three-quarter view. The hero object is tack sharp and the background melts into smooth, creamy blur on a seamless pale neutral sweep. Mood: calm, precise, orderly and quietly premium, like high-end editorial product photography. Strictly no people, figures, faces, hands or silhouettes. No readable text, letters, numbers, clock digits, logos, signage or user-interface graphics anywhere. No holograms, floating screens, robots with faces, dense cable tangles, carnival or circus elements, cartoon or plastic CGI look, oversaturated colour, lens flare or heavy vignette.

Photorealistic macro photograph of a handcrafted miniature tabletop diorama, captured mid-disaster. The same interview table now carries a teetering stack of ivory audit forms, clipboard after clipboard piled until the stack leans and sheets slide off its left side, frozen in a fan across the tabletop. The single chair has been pushed back and tipped onto two legs. Behind, every desk in the row now wears an ivory card tag on thread, and the first desk has been dragged out of line, its mug toppled and rolling, its jacket half off. The original lime tag hangs from the second desk, twisting on its thread. Loose forms have slid into the gaps between desks, marking a trail from the table to each one. Scuffed drag marks and paper dust follow the moved desk. Wide 16:9 landscape frame, same layout and angle as the calm version of this scene. The hero object stays slightly left of centre, and the spread of the disaster runs to the right and toward the camera so its path can be traced back to the source. Shot as a real physical model, not a 3D render. Materials are limited and tactile: heavyweight ivory cotton paper and card with visible fibres, soft folds and slightly deckled edges; matte, bead-blasted graphite metal with fine machining lines, chamfered edges and tiny hex fasteners; frosted acrylic with milky edges and a soft internal glow; sandblasted frosted glass. Surfaces carry believable imperfections: fine dust, paper grain, hairline creases, light scuffs on metal. Every object has convincing miniature scale and weight and rests firmly on its surface. Colour palette is restrained and nearly monochrome: white #FFFFFF, warm ivory, pale neutral #F3F5F2, soft grey-green #DCE1DA, muted graphite #626A64 and deep graphite #191D1B. Acid lime #D0F344 appears only on the lime element named in the scene, as the single signal colour, with olive #718D0B on its shadowed sides. Nothing else is lime or saturated; no red, orange or blue accents. Lighting: the same soft upper-left key and right-side bounce fill as a calm studio setup, unchanged, so the disorder reads as physical and real rather than theatrical. Airborne paper, grains and fragments catch the key light with crisp edge highlights. Camera: 85mm lens at f/5.6, same three-quarter tabletop angle, fast shutter freezing everything mid-air. Focus sits where the chain reaction started, and the spread softens into the depth of field. Mood: absurd but plausible, an orderly system that got out of hand, still clean and editorial. Photorealistic photograph of a vast handcrafted miniature landscape diorama. A wide flat plain of compacted ivory audit forms stretches to a hazy horizon, the sheets cracked and layered like dry mudflats. Across it stand long uneven rows of abandoned graphite desks, now the size of houses, like a field of markers, many tipped or sunk to their drawers, each with a bleached, frayed tag still hanging from it. The interview table lies overturned in the foreground, one leg snapped. In the midground, a slim graphite gantry sorter rides on two long rails above the rows, and its acid-lime grab is lifting one sound desk clear of the forms and setting it onto a flat graphite conveyor that carries a short line of restored desks toward a rebuilt, evenly spaced row. Wide 16:9 panoramic frame. The main ruin anchors the left or centre foreground, terrain rolls back to a distant horizon on the upper third, and the lime recovery rig sits in the right midground. Shot as a real physical model, not a 3D render. Surfaces carry believable imperfections: fine dust, paper grain, hairline creases, light scuffs on metal. Every object has convincing miniature scale and weight and rests firmly on its surface. Acid lime #D0F344 appears only on the lime element named in the scene, as the single signal colour, with olive #718D0B on its shadowed sides. Nothing else is lime or saturated; no red, orange or blue accents. Lighting: soft overcast late-afternoon daylight still falling from the upper left, with long soft shadows grounding the ruins and atmospheric haze fading distant forms into pale grey-green.
